title: I capped my x264 bitrate at 2M. Why is it still higher?

scenes.narration: You set dash max rate two M on a libx264 encode, and the bitrate comes out higher. Why? Max rate does nothing on its own. It needs dash buf size. We measure the average, and the busiest second.
captions: Why? We measure the average and the busiest second.

scenes.narration: The source is eight seconds of test pattern with noise: two hundred frames, hard to compress on purpose. Reader one is f f probe, packet sizes in a sliding one second window. Reader two copies the raw stream, and Node sums the frame sizes. With C R F eighteen alone, the average is three thousand five hundred eighty eight kilobits a second.
captions: Readers: ffprobe packets, raw stream in Node.

scenes.narration: Now add dash max rate two M. F f mpeg prints a warning: V B V max rate specified, but no buf size, ignored. The output is the same bytes. Same packet hash, same three thousand five hundred eighty eight, same busiest second, same quality. Spelling it two thousand K changes nothing.
captions: Warning: VBV maxrate specified, but no bufsize, ignored.

scenes.narration: Add dash buf size two M, and the encoder obeys. The average falls to two thousand ninety eight. The busiest second falls to two thousand five hundred ninety three, still above the cap. A four M buffer lets it climb to two thousand nine hundred forty two. The price is quality: P S N R falls from thirty seven point eight to thirty two point oh five dB.

A tiny buffer, two hundred K, is our control. The busiest second is two thousand seventy seven, so the readers can see a cap. Average mode, dash b v two M, honors the average, two thousand twenty four, but its busiest second is two thousand five hundred thirty one.
To cap a C R F encode, set both dash max rate and dash buf size, and check the busiest second, not only the average. Not tested: other presets, two pass, other encoders, real footage, and any player.
captions: Not tested: presets, two pass, real footage.
